title: VO₂max across sex and age
goal: Explain why women's VO₂max is on average lower than men's (haemoglobin, heart size, body composition), how VO₂max falls with age and what masters athletes keep, and judge how strong each piece of evidence is.

steps.title: A gap of about 10%
steps.text:
Men typically outperform women of similar age and training by 10–30%, depending on the event. The gap opens at puberty, when [testosterone](g:testosterone) rises about 30-fold in boys and stays low in girls [[c:hunter-gap]].

In endurance events the gap is at the low end: about **10–12%** across running distances [[c:sant-gap]]. VO₂max shows a similar gap. Even elite women's values are about 10% below those of elite men, per kg of body mass [[c:sant-elite]].

In absolute terms (L·min⁻¹) the gap is much bigger, because men are on average larger. Whatever the unit, these are averages: many trained women have a higher VO₂max than most men.

claims.text: Men typically outperform women by 10–30% in endurance, strength, speed and power events; the gap emerges at puberty as testosterone rises about 30-fold in males.

evidence.quote: Thus, for athletic events and sports relying on endurance, muscle strength, speed, and power, males typically outperform females by 10%-30% depending on the requirements of the event.

These sex differences in performance emerge with the onset of puberty and coincide with the increase in endogenous sex steroid hormones, in particular testosterone in males, which increases 30-fold by adulthood, but remains low in females.

claims.text: A 10–12% performance gap between men and women remains in all running distance events.

evidence.quote: there remains a 10-12% performance gap in all distance events

claims.text: Elite women's VO₂max is about 10% lower than that of elite men, per kg of body mass.

evidence.quote: Even truly elite women have VO2max values ~10% lower than those seen in men of similar elite status when expressed as mL/kg/min
with values in women typically averaging about 10% lower due to lower haemoglobin concentrations and higher levels of body fat

steps.title: Blood, heart and body composition
steps.text:
Three differences explain most of the gap [[c:sant-central]]:

| factor | women compared with men |
|---|---|
| [haemoglobin](g:haemoglobin) | about 12% lower concentration, and lower total mass |
| heart | smaller; lower maximal [stroke volume](g:stroke-volume), similar [HRmax](g:hrmax), so lower maximal cardiac output |
| body composition | more fat, so less muscle per kg |

The heart difference is partly body size: in college athletes, scaling heart mass to lean mass shrank much of it, though not fully in endurance athletes [[c:sant-lv]].

How much does blood explain? Blood was taken from men to bring their haemoglobin down to the women's level (153 to 134 g·L⁻¹). Their VO₂max fell about 7%, leaving most of the 47% absolute gap. Per kg of [fat-free mass](g:fat-free-mass), the sexes hadn't differed to begin with [[c:cureton]].

claims.text: Women typically have smaller hearts and lungs and lower haemoglobin than men, a mean haemoglobin about 12% lower, and lower maximal stroke volume with similar maximal heart rate.

evidence.quote: women typically have smaller hearts, lungs, and lower hemoglobin mass than men
Independent of iron status, women have mean hemoglobin levels of 12% lower than age and race-matched men
During high-intensity exercise, women reach lower maximal stroke volumes compared to men, resulting in a lower maximal cardiac output as maximal heart rate is similar across sexes.

claims.text: In college athletes, sex differences in left ventricular mass shrank or disappeared when scaled to lean body mass; in endurance athletes the difference remained significant after scaling.

evidence.quote: They found that the gender-related differences in left ventricular mass tended to decrease significantly or disappear, leading them to conclude that differences in left ventricular mass appear to be, to a large extent, related to differences in body composition
they found that in athletes from high intensity, or more endurance-driven sports, the differences between males and females remained significant despite scaling to lean body mass

claims.text: Lowering men's haemoglobin to the women's level reduced their VO₂max by about 7%: the haemoglobin difference explains a significant but relatively small part of the sex difference in absolute VO₂max; per kg of fat-free mass the sexes did not differ.

evidence.quote: Prior to blood withdrawal, VO2max expressed in L X min-1 and relative to body weight and ride time on the cycle ergometer test were greater (p less than .01) in men by 1.11 L X min-1 (47%), 4.8 ml X kg-1 min-1 (11.5%) and 5.9 min (67%), respectively, whereas VO2max expressed relative to fat-free weight (FFW) was not significantly different.
It was concluded that the sex difference in [Hb] accounts for a significant, but relatively small portion of the sex difference in VO2max (L X min-1).

steps.title: VO₂max per kg of fat-free mass
steps.problem: A cyclist weighs 60 kg, of which 12 kg is fat, and her VO₂max is 3.3 L·min⁻¹. What is her VO₂max per kg of fat-free mass?
steps: Fat-free mass = body mass − fat mass = 60 − 12 = 48 kg.
3.3 L·min⁻¹ × 1000 = 3,300 mL·min⁻¹; 3,300 ÷ 48 = 68.8 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ of fat-free mass.
Per kg of body mass it is 3,300 ÷ 60 = 55: the fat she carries lowers the usual figure, not her engine.

steps.title: Do women gain as much from training?
steps.text:
A meta-analysis pooled 8 studies that gave untrained men and women the same training (175 people). Men's VO₂max rose more: by about 190 mL·min⁻¹ more in absolute terms, and about 2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ more per kg [[c:dc-sex]].

One proposed reason is the heart. In one year-long study, women's heart mass stopped growing after about three months of training, while men's kept rising [[c:sant-lv-training]].

This is debated. The studies were few and small, all in untrained people. In the year-long study the women may have eaten too little for the training, and a plan matched for volume and intensity may simply suit men better [[c:sant-alt]]. Both sexes improve a lot: the reported difference is a fraction of the typical gain of about 5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹.

claims.text: In 8 studies of sex-matched endurance training (175 untrained people), VO₂max rose more in men than in women: by about 191 mL·min⁻¹ more in absolute terms and 1.95 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ more per kg.

evidence.quote: All studies implemented common modalities of ET in healthy untrained individuals, comprising a total of 175 men and women (90 ♂, 85 ♀).

After data pooling, ET induced substantially larger increases in absolute VO2max in men compared with women (mean difference = + 191 ml·min-1, 95% CI 99, 283; P < 0.001). A greater effect of ET on relative VO2max was also observed in men versus women (mean difference = + 1.95 ml·min-1·kg-1, 95% CI 0.76, 3.15; P = 0.001).

Pooled evidence demonstrates greater improvements in VO2max in healthy men compared with women in response to a given dose of ET, suggesting the presence of sexual dimorphism in the trainability of aerobic capacity.

claims.text: In a year of matched training, women's left ventricular mass reached its maximum after three months, while men's hypertrophy was more pronounced throughout.

evidence.quote: Females reached maximal left ventricular mass after only three months of training and did not show any further improvements.

claims.text: The smaller gains in women in the year-long study may partly reflect too little energy intake, and training plans matched for volume and intensity may suit men better than women.

evidence.quote: Thus, a possibility is that the lack of effect on VO 2max and cardiac mass could be due (in part) to a suboptimal energy intake in the female subjects
As the participants were matched for volume and intensity, there is also the possibility that the training protocol better suited the needs of the male vs. female subjects.

debate.question: Do men gain more VO₂max than women from the same training?

sides.position: Yes: pooled trials of matched training show larger gains in men, perhaps because men's hearts keep growing for longer.
Not clearly: the trials are few, small and in untrained people, and under-fuelling or plans built around men could explain the gap.

steps.title: Ageing: about 10% per decade
steps.text:
After about age 25–30, VO₂max falls by roughly **10% per decade** in healthy sedentary adults of both sexes [[c:ts-10pct]]. US reference data agree: from the 20s to the 70s, the median fell from 48.0 to 24.4 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ in men and from 37.6 to 18.3 in women [[c:friend-decline]].

The fall isn't steady, though. A [cohort study](g:cohort-study) followed 810 healthy adults for a median of 8 years. The loss sped up from 3–6% per decade in the 20s and 30s to more than 20% per decade in the 70s, at every level of reported leisure-time activity [[c:fleg]].

[Cross-sectional](g:cross-sectional-study) comparisons of age groups, which most of the older estimates come from, miss that acceleration and give a rosier picture.

claims.text: VO₂max declines by about 10% per decade after age 25–30 in healthy sedentary adults of both sexes.

evidence.quote: declines approximately 10% per decade after age 25–30 years in healthy sedentary adults of both sexes
The rate of decline in this cohort during a 5-decade period was approximately 10% per decade.

claims.text: In FRIEND, median VO₂max fell from 48.0 to 24.4 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ in men and from 37.6 to 18.3 in women between ages 20–29 and 70–79.

evidence.quote: In FRIEND, the 50th percentile VO 2max of men and women aged 20 to 29 years decreased from 48.0 and 37.6 mLO2 · kg(-1) · min(-1) to 24.4 and 18.3 mLO2 · kg(-1) · min(-1) for ages 70 to 79 years, respectively.

claims.text: Followed over time, VO₂peak decline accelerated from 3–6% per decade in the 20s and 30s to over 20% per decade in the 70s, at all levels of self-reported leisure-time activity; cross-sectional estimates may be overly optimistic.

evidence.quote: the rate of decline accelerated from 3% to 6% per 10 years in the 20s and 30s to >20% per 10 years in the 70s and beyond

Similar longitudinal rates of decline prevailed when peak VO2 was indexed per kilogram of body weight or per kilogram of fat-free mass and in all quartiles of self-reported leisure-time physical activity.
its rate of decline has been estimated primarily from cross-sectional studies that may provide misleading, overly optimistic estimates of aging changes

steps.title: Masters athletes: higher, not slower to fall
steps.text:
[Masters athletes](g:masters-athlete) keep far higher VO₂max values than sedentary people of their age. But their *percentage* loss per decade is not smaller, and in mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ it is larger, because they start higher [[c:ts-masters]].

What falls is every term of the [Fick equation](g:fick-principle): maximal heart rate, maximal stroke volume (to 80–90% of young athletes') and the [a-vO₂ difference](g:a-vo2-difference) [[c:ts-mech]]. Peak race performance holds until about 35, eases until 50–60, then drops faster [[c:ts-performance]].

Part of the fall is training: older athletes tend to train less and slower, and that explains much of the decline [[c:ts-training]]. People who keep training hard can hold VO₂max fairly steady for up to a decade in mid-life [[c:ts-maintain]].

claims.text: In habitually trained adults the percentage decline in VO₂max with age is not smaller than in sedentary adults, and the absolute decline (mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹) is larger.

evidence.quote: However, we and others subsequently established that when expressed as per cent decrease from early adulthood, the rate of decline in [V̇O2max] with age is not reduced in healthy adults who habitually perform aerobic exercise
In fact, endurance exercise-trained men and women demonstrate greater ‘absolute’ (ml kg−1 min−1) rates of decline in [V̇O2max] with age than healthy sedentary adults

claims.text: Falls in maximal stroke volume (to 80–90% of young trained adults), maximal heart rate and a-vO₂ difference all contribute to the lower VO₂max of older endurance athletes.

evidence.quote: Decreases in maximal stroke volume, heart rate and arterio-venous O(2) difference all appear to contribute to the age-related reductions in [V̇O2max] in endurance-trained athletes.
In older endurance exercise-trained adults, maximal stroke volume is reduced modestly to 80–90% of that observed in young endurance-trained adults

claims.text: Peak endurance performance is maintained until about 35 years, declines modestly until 50–60, then more steeply.

evidence.quote: Peak endurance performance is maintained until approximately 35 years of age, followed by modest decreases until 50-60 years of age, with progressively steeper declines thereafter.

claims.text: Age-related declines in endurance performance and its determinants appear largely mediated by lower training intensity and volume.

evidence.quote: Declines in endurance exercise performance and its physiological determinants with ageing appear to be mediated in large part by a reduction in the intensity (velocity) and volume of the exercise that can be performed during training sessions.

claims.text: Longitudinal studies suggest VO₂max can be fairly well maintained for up to 10 years in middle age by people who keep training vigorously.

evidence.quote: the results of longitudinal studies suggest that [V̇O2max] can be fairly well maintained over phases of middle-age lasting up to 10 years in men and women who continue to train vigorously

points: Men outperform women by about 10–12% in endurance events, and elite women's VO₂max is about 10% lower per kg.
Lower haemoglobin, a smaller heart and more body fat explain most of the gap; per kg of fat-free mass it shrinks or vanishes.
Men may gain somewhat more VO₂max from the same training, but the evidence is small and both sexes gain a lot.
VO₂max falls about 10% per decade from age 25–30, faster in old age; following people over time shows the acceleration.
Masters athletes stay far above sedentary peers but lose a similar percentage; keeping training volume and intensity up slows the fall.

variants.stem: Per kg of body mass, about how much lower is the VO₂max of elite female endurance athletes than that of elite men?

options.text: About 10%
options.why: Right: elite women's values average about 10% lower in mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹.

options.text: About 30%
options.why: 30% is the top of the range of sex gaps across all sports, mostly strength and power events.

options.text: About 47%
options.why: A gap of that size appears in absolute L·min⁻¹, where body size counts, not per kg.

options.text: No difference once trained
options.why: Even at the elite level a gap of about 10% remains.

variants.stem: Which difference helps explain why women's maximal cardiac output is lower than men's?

options.text: A smaller heart giving a lower maximal stroke volume
options.why: Right: maximal heart rate is similar, so the lower cardiac output comes from stroke volume.

options.text: A much lower maximal heart rate
options.why: Maximal heart rate is similar in women and men.

options.text: A higher haemoglobin concentration
options.why: Women's haemoglobin is about 12% lower, not higher; it lowers O₂ per litre, not cardiac output.

options.text: More capillaries per muscle fibre
options.why: Capillaries are a peripheral factor; they don't set cardiac output.

variants.stem: Which difference lowers how much O₂ each litre of a woman's blood carries, compared with a man's?

options.text: About 12% less haemoglobin per litre
options.why: Right: less haemoglobin per litre means less O₂ per litre.

options.text: A lower maximal heart rate in women
options.why: Maximal heart rate is similar, and it affects flow, not O₂ per litre.

options.text: A smaller stroke volume
options.why: Stroke volume sets how much blood is pumped, not how much O₂ each litre holds.

options.text: More body fat
options.why: Body fat lowers VO₂ per kg of body mass, not the O₂ in each litre of blood.

variants.stem: When men's haemoglobin was lowered to the women's level, their VO₂max fell about 7%, but most of the 47% gap in absolute VO₂max remained. What does this show?

options.text: Hb explains a small part; body and heart size matter more
options.why: Right: equalising Hb closed only a small share of the gap.

options.text: Haemoglobin explains all of the sex difference in VO₂max
options.why: If it did, matching Hb would have closed the gap.

options.text: Haemoglobin has no effect on VO₂max
options.why: VO₂max did fall 7% when Hb was lowered, so it matters, just not most.

options.text: Women have a higher VO₂max once Hb is matched
options.why: The men still had a much higher absolute VO₂max after matching.

variants.stem: A female triathlete: VO₂max 3.0 L·min⁻¹, 60 kg, 15 kg of fat. A male triathlete: 4.2 L·min⁻¹, 75 kg, 12 kg of fat. What is each one's VO₂max per kg of fat-free mass?

options.text: Both about 67 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: Right: 3,000 ÷ 45 = 66.7 and 4,200 ÷ 63 = 66.7. The gap per kg of body mass (50 vs 56) disappears.

options.text: Hers 50, his 56
options.why: These are per kg of body mass (3,000 ÷ 60 and 4,200 ÷ 75); subtract the fat first.

options.text: Hers 200, his 350
options.why: This divides by fat mass instead of fat-free mass.

options.text: Hers 67, his 56
options.why: This mixes the two: fat-free mass for her, body mass for him.

variants.stem: A female runner: VO₂max 2.8 L·min⁻¹, 55 kg, 14 kg of fat. A male runner: 3.9 L·min⁻¹, 70 kg, 10 kg of fat. What is each one's VO₂max per kg of fat-free mass?

options.text: Hers about 68, his 65
options.why: Right: 2,800 ÷ 41 = 68.3 and 3,900 ÷ 60 = 65.0. Per kg of body mass she is lower (51 vs 56).

options.text: Hers about 51, his 56
options.why: These are per kg of body mass; subtract the fat first.

options.text: Hers 200, his 390
options.why: This divides by fat mass instead of fat-free mass.

options.text: Hers 65, his 68
options.why: The values are swapped: her fat-free mass is 41 kg, his 60 kg.

variants.stem: A coach reads that men gained more VO₂max than women from the same training, and concludes that VO₂max work is not worth it for his female runners. What is the best judgement?

options.text: Wrong: women gain a lot too, and the extra gain in men is small and uncertain
options.why: Right: the pooled difference was about 2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ against gains of about 5, from 8 small studies.

options.text: Right: women barely respond to endurance training
options.why: Women improved substantially in these studies; the difference was in how much.

options.text: Right: the meta-analysis proves women can't raise VO₂max
options.why: It compared the size of gains; it didn't find women's gains to be zero.

options.text: Wrong: women gain more than men
options.why: The pooled studies found the opposite, though the evidence is limited.

variants.stem: A meta-analysis of 8 studies (175 untrained people) finds that men's VO₂max rose more than women's with the same training. What most limits how far this can be generalised?

options.text: Few, small studies, all in untrained people
options.why: Right: whether it holds in trained athletes, or with other training, isn't known.

options.text: Meta-analyses can never be trusted
options.why: Meta-analyses are high on the evidence ladder; the issue is what they pool.

options.text: Men and women can't be given the same training
options.why: The studies matched duration and intensity; that's what makes them comparable.

options.text: VO₂max can't be compared between the sexes
options.why: It can, in absolute or relative units; the issue is the evidence base.

variants.stem: A study compares cyclists aged 30, 50 and 70 at one point in time and concludes that VO₂max falls at a steady rate with age. What is the main weakness?

options.text: A snapshot misses that the decline speeds up
options.why: Right: longitudinal data found 3–6% per decade early on, over 20% in the 70s.

options.text: Cyclists don't lose any VO₂max with age
options.why: Trained people lose VO₂max with age too, by a similar percentage.

options.text: It should have used a placebo group
options.why: A placebo doesn't apply; the issue is the design, comparing different people once.

options.text: Age groups can't be compared at all
options.why: They can, but the snapshot mixes different generations and misses how the rate changes.

variants.stem: A running magazine shows VO₂max by age group from one survey and says each person will lose the same amount every decade. What is the main problem?

options.text: A snapshot can't show how the decline speeds up
options.why: Right: followed over time, the loss accelerates with age.

options.text: Runners were all measured on a treadmill
options.why: The test mode isn't the issue; the design is.

options.text: Women and men were pooled
options.why: Pooling may blur things, but the key flaw is the cross-sectional design.

options.text: The survey is too large to be reliable
options.why: A large sample isn't a weakness; the design is.

variants.stem: In endurance-trained athletes, what explains the fall in VO₂max with age?

options.text: Lower HRmax, stroke volume and a-vO₂ difference
options.why: Right: every term of the Fick equation falls a little.

options.text: Only the fall in maximal heart rate (HRmax)
options.why: HRmax was long seen as the main cause, but stroke volume and extraction fall too.

options.text: Only a smaller a-vO₂ difference
options.why: Extraction falls, but so do heart rate and stroke volume.

options.text: Worse running or cycling economy
options.why: Economy doesn't change with age in endurance-trained adults, and it doesn't set VO₂max.

variants.stem: A 45-year-old masters runner has a VO₂max of 60 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹; his sedentary brother has 35. Both keep their habits for 10 years. What is most likely?

options.text: Both lose about 10%: about 6 for him, about 3.5 for his brother
options.why: Right: the percentage loss is similar, so the fitter brother loses more mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, yet stays far higher.

options.text: The runner loses half as much percentage as his brother
options.why: Early studies suggested this, but later work found the percentage decline is not reduced in trained people.

options.text: The runner loses nothing while he keeps training
options.why: Training can hold VO₂max for a while in mid-life, but the age decline doesn't vanish.

options.text: Both lose exactly 6 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: The loss scales with the starting value; from 35, 10% is about 3.5.

variants.stem: A 50-year-old masters cyclist has a VO₂max of 55 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹; an inactive friend of the same age has 30. Over the next decade, which is most likely?

options.text: Similar % losses, so the cyclist loses more units
options.why: Right: about 10% each, so about 5.5 vs 3 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹; the cyclist stays far higher.

options.text: The cyclist's VO₂max stays the same as now
options.why: Even hard-training people lose VO₂max with age, though training slows it in mid-life.

options.text: The friend loses a much larger percentage
options.why: Percentage losses are similar in trained and sedentary adults.

options.text: Both end at the same value
options.why: The cyclist starts 25 higher; similar percentage losses keep most of that gap.

variants.stem: A 62-year-old triathlete's VO₂max fell 15% in 5 years, more than expected for her age. Over the same time she dropped her interval sessions and cut her weekly hours by half. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Much of it may be the lighter training, which she can change
options.why: Right: in masters athletes, falling training volume and intensity explain much of the decline.

options.text: It is all ageing, and nothing at all can be done
options.why: Ageing explains part, but reduced training is a large and changeable factor.

options.text: Her heart must be diseased
options.why: A faster fall with much less training doesn't point to disease; still, a doctor should check any worrying symptoms.

options.text: Her economy got worse, lowering her VO₂max
options.why: Economy doesn't set VO₂max and doesn't change with age in trained adults.

variants.stem: A 58-year-old runner who still trains hard and races every week kept his VO₂max almost unchanged between ages 48 and 56. What best explains this?

options.text: Hard training can hold VO₂max for years in mid-life
options.why: Right: in men and women who keep training vigorously, VO₂max can be fairly well maintained in middle age.

options.text: Runners simply don't age like other people
options.why: The age decline still comes; hard training delays it.

options.text: The tests must have been wrong
options.why: Holding VO₂max in mid-life is reported in longitudinal studies of hard-training adults.

options.text: VO₂max only starts to fall after 70
options.why: The decline usually starts at 25–30; it is just slow in mid-life for those who keep training.
